paper_title: FlowTranslator: Training-Free In-Image Machine Translation with Flow-Based Editing

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: In-image machine translation (IIMT) replaces text in an image with its translation while preserving the surrounding visual context. Existing task-specific models achieve convincing performance but require massive paired training images before and after translation. As advanced text-to-image (T2I) models have reached a practically usable level of multilingual text generation, we argue that this capability can be transferred to IIMT and present FlowTranslator. It is a training-free IIMT framework that first employs an OCR model and an LLM to generate the translation prompt, which is injected into the T2I-based diffusion model. To optimize the accurate and natural generation of translated text, we introduce two trajectory controls: Region Coupling Release (RCR) partially decorrelates target-branch noise inside the text region early in the trajectory, while Coupling Expansion (CE) amplifies the emerging edit displacement mid-trajectory. Under the EasyOCR read-back protocol, FlowTranslator achieves average PRIM BLEU and COMET scores of 20.6 and 57.2, respectively, substantially outperforming the strong training-based baseline UniTranslator. On the more challenging and realistic whole-image ScenePair photographs translated into Chinese, it reaches 40.1\% exact-match accuracy and surpasses existing editing systems, some of which only address the text-rendering stage rather than the complete IIMT task. These results establish flow-based editing as a strong, fully training-free baseline for IIMT.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: In-image machine translation (IIMT) translates the text embedded in an image and renders the translation back into the original text regions while keeping the rest of the image intact [15, 19]. The task underpins applications from mobile photo translation to localizing signage and product imagery, and has attracted dedicated benchmarks and models [18, 26, 27]. dominant line of work approaches IIMT with cascaded pipeline: an OCR model localizes and reads the source text, translation model converts it, and rendering module writes the translation back into the image [14, 47]. With the rapid advance of OCR and machine translation, the remaining bottleneck for this task is the rendering step. Early rendering systems erase the source glyphs and paste separately rendered text, procedure that leaves visible seams, mismatched typography, and destroyed textures. Subsequent work replaces the paste step with 1 Figure 1 Overview of the IIMT framework and editor paradigms. (a) The pipeline: OCR extracts text translator produces the translation scene text editor generates the output image. (b) Rule-based: remove, render, and paste separately. (c) Training-based: learned GAN or diffusion editor (requires extra training). (d) FlowTranslator (ours): training-free flow editing with trajectory controls (CE and RCR) for text translation with background preservation. learned scene-text-editing (STE) generator, first GAN-based [23, 32] and then diffusion-based [3, 28, 36], trained to blend the translated glyphs into the surrounding texture. However, these generators need paired images for training. Such cross-lingual pairs are scarce beyond handful of high-resource directions, so training pipelines fall back on synthetically rendered text [26], which narrows the fonts, layouts, and backgrounds the generator ever sees and leaves the fragile rendering step as the bottleneck of the cascade. Text-to-image (T2I) generation has meanwhile progressed to point where multilingual text rendering is usable in practice: recent flow-matching backbones render legible non-Latin and CJK (Chinese-Japanese-Korean) text directly from caption [41]. This raises natural question. Rather than training another dedicated STE generator on scarce cross-lingual pairs, can frozen T2I model be repurposed, with no task-specific training, to perform the rendering step of an IIMT cascade? Inversion-free flow editing offers exactly this machinery. FlowEdit [12] edits real image with frozen T2I flow model by integrating an ODE between source-conditioned branch and target-conditioned branch, and TextFlow [16] shows that such training-free editing can match trained scene-text editors in visual quality. Both operate on single word or crop given user-provided target string. Neither addresses the full IIMT problem of localizing, translating, and re-rendering every text region in an image automatically. Therefore, we propose FlowTranslator, novel IIMT system that requires no task-specific training. Every 2 module is frozen, publicly documented pretrained model, and no parameter is updated or fine-tuned for IIMT (the components themselves are, of course, products of large-scale pretraining). FlowTranslator keeps the modularity of cascade. general OCR model [4] finds text blocks, and frozen LLM translates them. The pipeline replaces the training-based rendering stage with region-masked flow editing on frozen T2I model [41]. The translation is generated into the original image rather than pasted onto it, so the diffusion prior handles perspective, lighting, and typography. Making this transfer work requires solving problem specific to cross-lingual, mask-confined editing: an ignition failure of the underlying flow editor. The FlowEdit update is driven by the velocity difference between the source-conditioned and target-conditioned branches, which share the same noise. The difference is meant to grow as the caption change propagates semantic edit. FlowEdit is demonstrated on edits, such as swapping an object or changing global style, that alter substantial fraction of the image and so produce an early, sizeable velocity difference. IIMT edits invert this premise. The text region is typically small minority of the frame, so the two branches barely differ at the outset and the edit never starts, no matter how the difference is subsequently amplified. This text-minority regime is intrinsic to cross-lingual scene-text editing rather than an artifact of our implementation, so generic remedy such as increasing the velocity gain cannot repair it: there is no signal left to amplify. We introduce two trajectory controls confined to the text-region mask to force ignition: Region Coupling Release (RCR) replaces the target-branch noise inside the mask with partially decorrelated sample early in the trajectory, giving the target branch room to diverge. Coupling Expansion (CE) amplifies the nascent edit displacement mid-phase, letting the target branch complete the edit it has started. Both add no forward passes and contribute zero latent update outside the mask. We evaluate FlowTranslator on three benchmarks spanning synthetic and real imagery, seven languages, and nine translation directions. It achieves the highest average BLEU on Translatotron-V(ision) [15] and the highest average BLEU and COMET on PRIM [26] without any IIMT training data. On ScenePair photographs translated into Chinese [23], FlowTranslator reaches 40.1% exact-match accuracy and outperforms six released editing systems under common evaluator. These results establish FlowTranslator as strong training-free baseline across diverse IIMT settings. In summary, our main contributions are: We repurpose frozen, training-free text-to-image flow model to replace the training-based rendering stage of IIMT cascades and remove its dependence on scarce cross-lingual training pairs. We identify an edit-ignition failure of coupled flow editing and propose two mask-confined trajectory controls (RCR and CE) without additional forward passes to resolve it. We report results on TTV, PRIM, and ScenePair competitive with trained systems, establishing strong training-free baseline for IIMT.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: In-image Machine Translation. Cascaded systems remain the dominant paradigm for IIMT, decomposing the task into OCR [46, 38, 46], machine translation, and text rendering [14, 33, 47]. This modular design has advanced alongside its components: stronger OCR [7, 37, 40] and translation models improve text recovery and translation, while the rendering stage has evolved from removing the source text and pasting separately rendered glyphs to learned scene-text editors that better preserve background, layout, and typography [3, 23, 28]. Cascades can therefore incorporate strong pretrained models and upgrade each stage independently, but they still suffer from error propagation, and rendering often remains the principal source of visual degradation. End-to-end IIMT has been explored as an alternative, from early pixel-level models [19] to Translatotron-V [15], VisTrans [26], and recent unified multimodal systems such as UniTranslator [18] and AnyTrans [22]. These recent models have narrowed the gap and report performance competitive with cascaded baselines on established benchmarks, showing the growing viability of unified modeling. However, all published full-pipeline IIMT systems we are aware of train or fine-tune at least one component on IIMT data, whereas FlowTranslator updates no parameters at all. 3 Figure 2 Overview of FlowTranslator. OCR extracts the source text and forms source caption, while frozen LLM translates it to obtain the target caption. frozen VAE encodes the source image into 𝑍src , from which noise initialization produces 𝑍FE . At each editing step, the same frozen DiT predicts sourceand target-conditioned velocities. Their 𝑇 difference updates the flow-editing latent. RCR perturbs the target-branch noise within the detected text region, and CE amplifies the accumulated displacement before it is fed back to the target branch. The final latent 𝑍FE is decoded to 0 produce the translated image. 0 Scene Text Editing. The rendering step of IIMT needs editors to replace words in images with GAN or diffusion models. Early systems transfer or regenerate text appearance with adaptive or stroke-level models [23, 25, 32, 35]. Recent diffusion editors [3, 13, 28, 39, 42, 44]. Recognition-aware editors further use text recognition to improve content fidelity, as in RS-STE [9]. For cross-lingual rendering, however, these editors need paired images showing the same scene rendered in both scripts. Such pairs are scarce beyond few high-resource directions, so training pipelines fall back on synthetically composited text [26], narrowing the appearance diversity seen in training. TextFlow [16] shows that training-free flow editing can match trained editors on word crops. Our work lifts training-free editing to the full IIMT task with automatic localization and translation. Training-free Flow Editing. Flow matching provides simulation-free training objective for continuous generative flows [17]. FlowEdit [12] constructs an inversion-free ODE between source and target text conditions of pretrained flow-matching model [2, 8] and is the foundation of our renderer. Other recent studies regularize rectified-flow trajectories or design training-free conditional samplers for image editing [11, 29, 45, 48], reflecting shift from constructing new ODEs to controlling them. Our RCR and CE belong to this family as spatially masked controls designed specifically for the text-minority ignition setting.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: This section describes how FlowTranslator turns frozen T2I model into renderer for in-image machine translation, following the pipeline shown in Fig. 2. FlowTranslator takes FlowEdit [12], an inversion-free editing procedure for pretrained flow-matching models, as its starting point. It then adds two trajectory controls that overcome an ignition failure particular to cross-lingual, mask-confined editing, so that multilingual text is rendered accurately without task-specific training or extra inference cost. No component in the pipeline is trained or fine-tuned.

sections.title: 3.2 Region Coupling Release
sections.content: Region Coupling Release (RCR) targets the root cause of the fixed point, the perfect noise correlation between the branches. Instead of feeding the target branch the source noise 𝜖, RCR feeds it partially decorrelated sample inside the mask. With schedule 𝑠(𝑡) ramping linearly from 1 (for 𝑡 𝜏hi) to 0 (for 𝑡 𝜏lo), we draw an independent 𝜖 𝒩 (0, 𝐼), fresh at every step and every noise sample like 𝜖, and form 𝜖tar = 𝜌 𝜖 + (cid:113) 1 𝜌2 𝜖, 𝜌 = 1 𝜅 𝑠(𝑡), (3) 5 𝑡 ˆ𝑧tar ˆ𝑧tar 𝑡 + 𝑀 𝑡 (𝜖tar 𝜖). (4) Inside the text region the target branch now sees noise that is only 𝜌-correlated with the source branch, so the two velocities are evaluated at genuinely different points and their difference stops vanishing. The edit has room to ignite. Three design choices govern this mechanism. First, the decorrelation is partial, 𝜅 < 1: Eq. (3) preserves the marginal distribution of 𝜖tar while interpolating its coupling strength, whereas full decorrelation would sever the branches and degrade the edit into mask-region regeneration. Second, the perturbation in Eq. (4) is additive on top of the accumulated displacement rather than an attenuation of it, so it preserves existing edit progress instead of rescaling the update and shrinking the edit along with the noise, as ordinary guidance schemes do. Third, the release follows schedule: it is widest early, for 𝑡 𝜏hi, where the trajectory is noise-dominated and divergence is cheap, and it closes completely for 𝑡 𝜏lo, restoring exact coupling so that late steps refine glyphs under the same conditions as vanilla FlowEdit. Together these choices let RCR open controlled window for divergence without discarding the coupling that grounds the edit in the source image.

sections.title: 3.3 Coupling Expansion
sections.content: RCR opens room to ignite but supplies no direction of its own, since decorrelated branch may drift toward any content consistent with the target caption. The needed direction is already present in the trajectory: the accumulated displacement 𝑍FE points from the source toward the emerging edit. Coupling Expansion (CE) feeds this displacement back into the target branch as positive feedback: 𝑡 𝑍src 0 𝑡 ˆ𝑧tar ˆ𝑧tar 𝑡 + 𝑐 sin2(𝜋𝑡) 𝑀 (𝑍FE 𝑡 𝑍src 0 ), (5) so the target branch is evaluated at point where the nascent edit already appears more advanced than it is. The conditional velocity then responds by completing that edit, and the loop closes on itself. The sin2 gate confines this feedback to the middle of the trajectory for structural reason. Early on, there is no displacement to expand because 𝑍FE , so CE stays inert on its own and cannot inject spurious direction before RCR has created one. Late in the trajectory, the gate closes again to keep runaway amplification from distorting glyph shapes during refinement. Our subsequent ablation (4.4) shows that CE alone carries most of the gain, while RCR adds further increment on top and composes positively with CE across most translation directions.

sections.title:
4.1 Evaluation and Implementation Details
Benchmarks. TTV (Translatotron-V(ision)) [15] contains 5122 synthetic text images built from IWSLT14/17.
Following the official splits, we evaluate De→En (3,526), En→De (3,524), Fr→En (4,925), and Ro→En (1,008).
PRIM [26] contains photographed real-world 512 × 46 text strips. We evaluate all five directions En→{De,
Fr, Cs, Ru, Ro} (340 each) against the official Google-translation references. ScenePair [23] provides 1,280
real scene photographs with English text. We translate every whole scene image into Chinese (En→Zh). For
a controlled comparison, all methods use the same text boxes and target translations, with each method
receiving them in its official input format. Fixing these upstream OCR and translation stages prevents their
errors from confounding the comparison. The resulting protocol isolates the rendering stage and measures
how reliably each method places the prescribed Chinese text within the specified image regions. Exact-match
ACC is computed by the recognizer of PP-OCRv6 [43].

For TTV, image quality is measured by SSIM against the source, using the structural-similarity formulation of Wang et al. [30]. To reduce sensitivity to initialization, we evaluate our configurations with multiple random seeds and report the mean across seeds. For each seed, the Avg. columns are then computed as unweighted means across translation directions. OCR read-back systematically underestimates rendered-text quality, and reader errors are attributed to the system under test. We report EasyOCR numbers in all comparisons for protocol parity. An LLM-bridged alignment check also found 1.4% of TTV DeEn reference lines locally misaligned by 1 line, shared defect of the reference files that shifts corpus BLEU on our outputs by well under one point. Implementation. We use Z-Image-Turbo [41], distilled 6B flow-matching T2I model, with 𝑇=50 steps and editing window 𝑛max=45. For all TTV and PRIM runs, we set RCR 𝜅=0.5 (𝜏hi=0.6, 𝜏lo=0.3), CE 𝑐=0.4, velocity gain 𝛾=1.3, and latent-mask dilation to 15%. Images are resized so the long side is 1024 using bicubic interpolation, with dimensions rounded to multiples of 16. PRIM strips are bicubic-upscaled to the same editing canvas (512 46 1024 80) and downscaled to their original size after editing. Text regions and recognized strings come from the PP-OCRv5 [4]. Translations and captions come from one call per image to commercial LLM (Doubao-Seed-2.0-lite). The LLM returns the translations embedded in pair of descriptive captions. The source caption 𝑐src describes the scene with the original strings in quotes. The target caption 𝑐tgt is identical except that the quoted strings are replaced by their translations. The prompt contains the image and the numbered OCR text lines. It asks the LLM to translate each line into concise target-language scene-text phrase and to return strict JSON with the translation pairs, one-sentence English source caption that quotes every source line verbatim, and target caption that changes only those quoted strings to their translations. The prompt also requires the original line order and all non-text scene descriptions to remain unchanged. All experiments are conducted on single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU.

For example, it scores 35.2 / 63.0 on EnDe versus 13.1 / 48.7 for UniTranslator. Z-Image-Turbos prior renders Cyrillic unreliably, producing near-Latin glyph substitutions that OCR cannot read and resulting in 4.6 BLEU. Training-free operation inherits the script coverage of the frozen backbone.

sections.title:
4.4 Ablations
Trajectory Controls. Holding the pipeline, masks, prompts, and all other hyperparameters fixed, adding RCR
and CE raises average PRIM BLEU from 16.88 to 20.57, a relative gain of 22%. The two single-mechanism
arms show where this gain comes from. CE alone already recovers 3.33 of the full 3.69-point improvement,
roughly 90% of the total. RCR is nonetheless not redundant: it composes positively with CE on four of the
five directions, and only on En→Ru does adding RCR on top of CE cost a small amount, lowering BLEU from
5.03 to 4.57. This division of labor matches the mechanism described in §3: CE supplies the direction that
drives most of the edit, while RCR supplies the room for that direction to act.

For each example, we show the source image (with red boxes marking text to be translated), the requested target text, and outputs of existing open-source methods, followed by FlowTranslator. FlowTranslator renders the requested Chinese text within the original region. It preserves both the surrounding scene and the local text appearance. it to 48 over-edits the region and destroys layout, dropping BLEU further to 14.99. We use 𝑛max=45 for 𝑇=50 in all other experiments as the setting that balances these two failure modes. The trajectory controls and the edit window act on different benchmarks in consistent direction. On ScenePair, adding the controls raises exact-match ACC from 33.44% to 40.08% (Tab. 3), the same pattern of improvement seen on PRIM. Cross-benchmark Analysis. Across benchmarks, the relative gain from the trajectory controls tracks how hard the edit is to ignite. The gain is largest on PRIM, where the translated text occupies small, photographic strip of the image (+22% relative average BLEU). But it is smallest on TTV, where the text is large, clean, and synthetic (+2% on RoEn, its most affected direction). The benchmarks differ in more than text-area ratio, so this pattern is consistent with the ignition interpretation that hard-to-ignite, small-glyph regimes benefit most from explicit trajectory intervention. Importantly, the same control configuration is used across benchmarks, so the difference in gains does not arise from benchmark-specific tuning. The agreement between PRIM BLEU and ScenePair exact-match ACC further shows that the controls improve text completion under both strip-level and whole-image evaluation.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented FlowTranslator, training-free IIMT framework. It replaced the trained rendering stage of an IIMT cascade with region-masked flow editing on frozen text-to-image model. Two mask-confined trajectory controls, Region Coupling Release and Coupling Expansion, resolved an ignition failure specific to the text-minority regime of cross-lingual editing. Under the EasyOCR read-back protocol, FlowTranslator attained the highest reported average BLEU and COMET on PRIM. It also attained the highest average BLEU on Translatotron-V(ision), all without any IIMT training data. On real ScenePair photographs translated into Chinese, it reached 40.1% exact-match accuracy, exceeding six released editing systems. Once its branch coupling was corrected for the text-minority regime, frozen T2I flow model could match or exceed systems trained on millions of IIMT pairs. This established flow-based editing as strong training-free baseline for IIMT. The method still inherited the script coverage of its frozen backbone, and Cyrillic rendering failed in our experiments. Extending the trajectory controls to backbones with broader script support remains direction for future work.

sections.content: This appendix provides trajectory-level diagnostics for the two mask-confined controls introduced in the main text. Using four matched arms (Masked FlowEdit (denoted as FlowEdit in the figures), +RCR, +CE, and +RCR+CE), we test whether RCR relaxes early branch coupling and whether CE amplifies the accumulated displacement without destabilizing the latent trajectory. CE-off arms lie at zero. (d) Paired per-step difference in the latent maximum relative to Masked FlowEdit. Global maxima for Masked FlowEdit and +RCR+CE differ by 1.6%. Final edit displacement. This division of labor matches the mechanism: RCR alone changes the final displacement by only +0.7% and primarily affects edit onset, whereas CE affects final magnitude. Using an ignition threshold shared by all arms (the first step at which 𝑑in(𝑡) reaches 10% of the Masked FlowEdit arms final displacement on the same image), the edit departs from the source at step 9.50 for the baseline and 7.75 under RCR, i.e. 1.75 steps earlier, earlier on 9/12 images, later on 1/12 and tied on 2/12 (𝑝 = 0.021). +CE alone reaches 9.42 while +RCR+CE reaches 7.67, earlier on 10/12 (𝑝 = 0.012) (Fig. S2(a,b)). Across different source languages and text layouts, FlowTranslator replaces the selected source text with the requested Chinese translation while preserving the surrounding scene and the local appearance of the text region. These cases are consistent with the trajectory diagnostics above: the controls strengthen the edit within the detected text mask, while the background remains unchanged in latent space.
